cues.text: A Farmer's Devotion, Not His Malice

Unlike most medieval Eucharistic accounts, which typically begin with an act of theft meant to desecrate or profit from the Blessed Sacrament, the tradition of Bettbrunn begins with something closer to misguided love.
A farmer living at a small holding then called Viehbrunn, in Bavaria, was known for his deep devotion to the Eucharist.
Tradition relates that he lived roughly an hour and a half from his parish church at Tholling and could not always attend Mass as often as he wished.
His solution, however well-intentioned, was itself an act of theft.
He began secretly carrying a consecrated host home, concealed in the hollow end of his walking stick.
Each day, while his cattle grazed, he planted it in the ground so that he could kneel in adoration before it.
A Host That Would Not Be Lifted
For months, the account holds, the farmer continued in this way undetected.
Then one day, distracted while driving his herd, he struck his stick into the ground without thinking, and the host fell from it onto the earth.
Try as he might, tradition says, he could not lift it back up.
Word of the strange occurrence reached the parish priest at Tholling, who came and likewise found himself unable to raise the host from the ground.
A Bishop's Vow
At last, tradition relates, Bishop Hartwich of Regensburg came to the spot in person with his clergy.
He too found the host would not be moved—until he vowed that, if permitted to lift it, he would have a chapel built on that very place in its honor.
Only then, the account holds, was the host finally raised.
The village of Bettbrunn and its Church of the Holy Savior grew up around that promise.
The account of the farmer's devotion, however imperfectly it began, became the founding story of a pilgrimage site that has drawn the faithful of Bavaria for nine centuries.
A Later Written Record
The earliest surviving written version of this account dates only to around 1420, roughly three centuries after its traditional setting in 1125.
In the careful language of tradition, this gap places it among later medieval accounts rather than a contemporary record, whose precise historical details cannot be independently verified.
Legacy
We find something quietly instructive in a tradition that begins not with hatred of the Eucharist, as so many medieval accounts do.
Instead, it begins with a love for the Eucharist strong enough to lead an ordinary farmer into wrongdoing he likely never fully reasoned through.
His story does not excuse the theft at its center, but it does remind us that even disordered devotion can be the raw material God uses to draw a whole community closer to the altar.
Nine centuries later, the church built on a bishop's promise still stands as a testament to a hunger for the Eucharist that, however clumsily expressed, refused to be satisfied by distance alone.
